heading_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook
jurisdiction: international evidence, applicability should be localized to Jakarta
publisher: World Health Organization, Regional Office for Europe
section_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook
text:
Published: 2024-10-04
Status as of: 2026-09-07 (health guidance; not Indonesian law)
Document type: health_guidance
Tags: topic=exposure-protection; audience=Jakarta-resident; action=protect-now; pollutant=ambient-particles
title: Bad-air-day protection playbook

heading_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > What to do now
jurisdiction: international evidence, applicability should be localized to Jakarta
publisher: World Health Organization, Regional Office for Europe
section_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > What to do now
text:
1. Check a fresh reading and timestamp on the official DKI portal (and the
   pollutant, not only the index). If the reading is elevated, shorten outdoor
   time, move exercise to a cleaner time/place, and avoid moderate-to-vigorous
   outdoor exertion. Jakarta's own seasonal notice says low rain and wind in
   the dry season can allow PM2.5 to accumulate; this is local context, not a
   forecast for every day.
2. Make the cleanest indoor room the place where children, older adults, and
   people with heart or lung disease spend more time. Keep windows and doors
   closed while outdoor particles are higher, but ventilate when outdoor air is
   cleaner. Closing windows is not a complete solution: cooking, tobacco,
   incense, candles, and other indoor sources can still raise exposure.
3. If a short, unavoidable high-particle exposure requires a respirator, use a
   certified, approved particulate respirator (for example an approved N95 or
   equivalent) that seals over the nose and mouth. Put it on correctly, keep it
   on throughout exposure, replace it when saturated or damaged, and do not
   treat a loose surgical/cloth mask as equivalent. A particulate respirator
   does not remove gases, and a poor seal defeats the rating.
4. For indoor particles, a portable cleaner can help when it is sized for the
   room, operated at a useful fan speed, and maintained. It supplements source
   control and cleaner-air ventilation; it cannot make a room pollutant-free.
title: Bad-air-day protection playbook

heading_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > Limits and escalation
jurisdiction: international evidence, applicability should be localized to Jakarta
publisher: World Health Organization, Regional Office for Europe
section_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > Limits and escalation
text:
WHO's review found portable filters can lower indoor PM2.5 in real-world
studies, but health evidence is limited and devices have cost, noise,
maintenance, infiltration, and ozone/gas-removal limitations. It found little
evidence of health benefit from respirators in the general public and does not
recommend routine respirator use as a population measure; short controlled
high-exposure situations are a different risk-management question. People with
cardiorespiratory disease should ask a clinician before using a respirator or
changing activity. This assistant cannot diagnose symptoms. Seek urgent care
for severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting, blue lips, or rapidly
worsening symptoms; persistent or concerning symptoms warrant a clinician.
title: Bad-air-day protection playbook

heading_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > Limits and escalation
jurisdiction: international evidence, applicability should be localized to Jakarta
publisher: World Health Organization, Regional Office for Europe
section_path: Bad-air-day protection playbook > Limits and escalation
text:
Personal protection reduces a person's dose. It does not reduce Jakarta's
emissions and cannot replace enforcement or clean-air policy. [bad-air-day-protection]
title: Bad-air-day protection playbook

heading_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles are general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room
text:
Published: not stated; page last updated 2026-02-17 (accessed 2026-09-07)
Status as of: 2026-09-07 (technical guidance; not Indonesian law)
Document type: indoor_air_guidance
Tags: topic=indoor-filtration; audience=household; action=protect-now; pollutant=particles
title: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room

heading_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Selecting and operating filtration
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles are general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Selecting and operating filtration
text:
Choose a portable cleaner with a clean-air delivery rate (CADR) appropriate to
the room; a larger room or higher ceiling needs more clean-air delivery. EPA's
example sizing table for an eight-foot ceiling is 65 cfm for 100 square feet,
130 cfm for 200, 195 cfm for 300, and 390 cfm for 600. Treat these as sizing
estimates, not a guarantee for a Jakarta home. Run the unit at a fan speed
that occupants can tolerate, place it near the breathing zone of the people
most at risk, and replace a loaded filter. For a central HVAC system, EPA says
to use at least MERV 13 or the highest rating the fan can safely handle; a
technician may be needed to check pressure and fit.
title: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room

heading_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Selecting and operating filtration
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles are general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Selecting and operating filtration
text:
CADR is a particle-cleaning rate, not proof that a device removes gases. A
particle filter/HEPA unit will not remove all pollutants; activated carbon can
help with some gases only when there is enough sorbent material, and there is
no widely used gas-performance rating. Avoid ozone-generating devices and do
not make claims that an ionizer, plant, fragrance, or a cheap “HEPA-like” label
will protect against every pollutant.
title: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room

heading_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Clean-air-room tradeoffs
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles are general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Clean-air-room tradeoffs
text:
During a particle episode, close windows and doors when outdoor air is dirtier
than indoor air and use filtration. When outdoor air is cleaner, ventilate to
remove indoor-generated particles and carbon dioxide. Always control indoor
sources: do not smoke or burn incense indoors, use a range hood vented outside
when safe, and avoid frying or other high-particle activities in the clean
room. A cleaner does not compensate for a combustion source in the room.
title: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room

heading_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Clean-air-room tradeoffs
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles are general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room > Clean-air-room tradeoffs
text:
EPA states that no cleaner removes all pollutants and that effectiveness
depends on room size, filter efficiency, airflow, run time, infiltration,
maintenance, and indoor sources. [clean-air-room]
title: Indoor filtration and a clean-air room

heading_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Scope
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles may be general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Scope
text: The EPA guide discusses portable air cleaners, heating/ventilation and air-conditioning filters, indoor pollutant sources and practical limits. It is technical household guidance and should not be presented as a Jakarta regulation.
title: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition)

heading_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > CADR and room size
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles may be general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > CADR and room size
text: The guide explains that a portable cleaner's clean air delivery rate (CADR) and the room size determine how much filtered air is delivered. A product recommendation therefore needs room dimensions and a stated particle CADR, rather than only a marketing label.
title: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition)

heading_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > HVAC filtration
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles may be general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > HVAC filtration
text: The guide discusses higher-efficiency HVAC filters, including MERV 13 where the system can accommodate the pressure drop. Compatibility, fit, operating time and maintenance affect delivered filtration; a filter rating alone does not guarantee a measured indoor concentration.
title: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition)

heading_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Indoor sources and cautions
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles may be general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Indoor sources and cautions
text: The guide also identifies indoor sources and notes that filtration does not remove every pollutant. Smoking, cooking, incense, candles and other combustion sources should be reduced or controlled, while ventilation decisions should account for outdoor conditions.
title: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition)

heading_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Locator note
jurisdiction: United States technical guidance; engineering principles may be general
publisher: United States Environmental Protection Agency
section_path: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition) > Locator note
text: Use the EPA page section heading and relevant table/paragraph for an exact citation. This source supports engineering and indoor-air explanations only; it cannot establish health outcomes or legal requirements in Jakarta.
title: US EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home (2nd edition)

heading_path: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution
text:
People can reduce exposure by checking a fresh local observation, changing the
time or location of strenuous outdoor activity, and reducing intense exercise
during high-pollution episodes. Staying indoors helps only when indoor sources
are controlled and outdoor particles are not being drawn inside.
title: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution

heading_path: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution
text:
A properly fitted, certified particulate respirator can reduce inhaled
particles such as PM2.5, but it does not remove every gas and fit is important.
Portable particle filtration may reduce indoor PM2.5, but effectiveness depends
on room size, filter performance, fan speed, infiltration, maintenance, cost,
and indoor sources. People with relevant medical conditions should seek advice
from a qualified clinician. This information supports exposure decisions and
does not diagnose an individual.
title: Reducing personal exposure to air pollution

heading_path: Health communication boundary
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: Health communication boundary
text:
Air-quality information can support exposure-reduction decisions, but it does
not diagnose an individual. The assistant should provide educational information,
state uncertainty, and direct people with severe or persistent symptoms to a
qualified healthcare professional.
title: Health communication boundary

heading_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability
jurisdiction: international evidence adapted to Jakarta context
publisher: World Health Organization; Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta
section_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability
text:
Published: 2024-11-15 (WHO practical briefs); DKI programme guidance accessed 2026-09-07
Status as of: 2026-09-07 (recommendations and programmes; not a substitute for enforcement)
Document type: civic_and_emissions_guidance
Tags: topic=individual-contribution; audience=Jakarta-resident; action=reduce-emissions; action=accountability
title: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability

heading_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions with a plausible direct emissions pathway
jurisdiction: international evidence adapted to Jakarta context
publisher: World Health Organization; Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta
section_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions with a plausible direct emissions pathway
text:
Use public transport, shared trips, walking, or cycling where current air
quality, heat, safety, and mobility needs make that reasonable. Avoid needless
idling, maintain the engine and tyres, repair visible smoke, and complete the
required emissions test; a passing test is a compliance action, not proof that
one vehicle explains a citywide episode. Do not burn household waste or leaves
in the open. Reduce indoor combustion and choose cleaner household fuels and
efficient equipment where feasible. These choices can reduce a person's or
household's emissions, but their citywide effect depends on adoption and
system design.
title: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability

heading_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions that influence structural change
jurisdiction: international evidence adapted to Jakarta context
publisher: World Health Organization; Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta
section_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions that influence structural change
text:
Report suspected open burning, smoky vehicles, or industrial violations through
the responsible DKI/KLHK reporting channel and keep the date, location, photo
or video, wind/odour description, and the relevant station reading. Join a
community-monitoring project only if sensors have documented calibration and
do not present a low-cost sensor as an official regulatory measurement. Ask
officials for inspection coverage, test-pass/fail and sanction counts, CEMS
data, source inventories, budgets, and implementation milestones. Participate
in consultations and local planning, and compare promises with dated public
reports.
title: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability

heading_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions that influence structural change
jurisdiction: international evidence adapted to Jakarta context
publisher: World Health Organization; Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta
section_path: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability > Actions that influence structural change
text:
WHO's hierarchy is important: personal interventions can reduce short-term
exposure, but public policies that reduce emissions are more effective,
sustainable, and equitable. Protecting yourself on a bad day and reducing your
own emissions are different goals; neither makes an individual responsible for
structural enforcement gaps. [individual-emission-actions]
title: What an individual can do to reduce emissions and improve accountability

heading_path: Indonesian ISPU categories
publisher: Ministry of Environment and Forestry
section_path: Indonesian ISPU categories
text:
The Indonesian ISPU categories used in this demo are Baik (1-50), Sedang
(51-100), Tidak Sehat (101-200), Sangat Tidak Sehat (201-300), and Berbahaya
(301 or higher). ISPU is an index without a physical concentration unit.
title: Indonesian ISPU categories

heading_path: Indonesian ISPU categories
publisher: Ministry of Environment and Forestry
section_path: Indonesian ISPU categories
text:
Never describe an ISPU value as a PM2.5 concentration. The application should
show the index and the concentration separately.
title: Indonesian ISPU categories

heading_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta / Vital Strategies / ITB
section_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
text:
Jakarta's pollution has multiple local and regional sources. The 2020 DKI
emissions inventory attributed major shares of NOx, CO, PM10, and PM2.5
emissions to transport, while manufacturing was the largest source of SO2 and
a major secondary source for particulate pollution. These are emissions-
inventory estimates, not a direct measurement of a person's exposure.
title: What causes Jakarta air pollution

heading_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta / Vital Strategies / ITB
section_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
text:
The 2019–2020 Jakarta/ITB/Vital Strategies receptor-based source-apportionment
study found that transport contributed substantially to ambient PM2.5, with
different estimates by season and sampling site. It also identified coal
combustion, construction, open burning, soil, and road dust. Emissions
inventory and receptor apportionment answer different questions and should not
be collapsed into one universal percentage. Wind, rainfall, atmospheric mixing,
season, and sources outside DKI can change observed concentrations.
title: What causes Jakarta air pollution

heading_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta / Vital Strategies / ITB
section_path: What causes Jakarta air pollution
text:
The evidence supports statements about likely contributors, not a claim that a
single source caused one station's reading. Current station observations are
descriptive and should be interpreted with their timestamp, location, and
quality metadata.
title: What causes Jakarta air pollution

DLH describes continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS) as a way to
measure and calculate emissions released from stacks in near real time. Its
public monitoring page lists operational-control and evaluation reports for
stationary sources for 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024, including a 2024

title: Stationary-source emissions monitoring (CEMS)

heading_path: Stationary-source emissions monitoring (CEMS)
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta
section_path: Stationary-source emissions monitoring (CEMS)
text:
The existence of reports demonstrates monitoring activity, not that every
industrial stack is covered, every reading is compliant, or corrective orders
were completed. A useful implementation dashboard should publish the regulated
source denominator, uptime and missingness, exceedances, inspections, orders,
sanctions, and closure dates. [jakarta-cems-monitoring]
title: Stationary-source emissions monitoring (CEMS)

heading_path: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta
section_path: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation
text:
DLH DKI's FAQ says emissions testing is mandatory for individual passenger
cars and motorcycles older than three years under Pergub 66/2020. It also
describes a traffic-ticket consequence for vehicles that fail, under the
national traffic-law framework. The rule, a test result, a roadside inspection,
and an actual sanction are different events; a legal obligation alone does not
show the share of vehicles tested or repaired.
title: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation

heading_path: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta
section_path: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation
text:
For accountability, publish the eligible-vehicle denominator, test-centre
capacity and calibration, pass/fail and retest counts, roadside-check coverage,
and sanction follow-through by period. No complete denominator or independent
compliance rate is asserted here because it is not supplied by this FAQ.
[jakarta-emission-testing]
title: Jakarta vehicle-emissions testing obligation

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality
text:
API source: https://air-quality-api.open-meteo.com/v1/air-quality
Retrieved: 2026-09-07
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > What the two lines are
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > What the two lines are
text:
`pm2_5` and `pm10` are separate Open-Meteo Air Quality API variables, both in
µg/m³. They are CAMS global model concentrations near the surface at the
Jakarta coordinate (-6.2088, 106.8456), not DKI station measurements or ISPU
values. The CAMS global product is a roughly 0.4° (about 45 km), 3-hourly model
grid. The Zenodo record covers 2022-08-01 through 2026-02-18; the repository
also contains a separately labelled Open-Meteo refresh from 2026-06-07 through
2026-09-06.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > What the two lines are
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > What the two lines are
text:
The retained CSV is daily. For the repository's recent refresh, ingestion
groups the API timestamps by local Asia/Jakarta date and averages each
pollutant independently over its available upstream values. The Zenodo
artifact supplies daily date rows, but does not retain raw timestamps or
document its per-day sample count in the metadata available here; its original
resampling method is therefore an evidence gap. Missing PM10 is not filled
from PM2.5, and vice versa. No forward-fill, interpolation, or ISPU conversion
is applied.
The chart sends the stored daily rows directly to the line series; it does not
aggregate them again. The station trend view is a separate data layer.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
text:
The file has 1,390 distinct dates from 2022-08-01 to 2026-09-06, with a
108-day coverage gap after 2026-02-18 before the refresh begins on 2026-06-07.
Each pollutant has 1,387 non-missing values and three missing values; the
paired rows are therefore observations/dates, not station readings. PM2.5 has
mean/median
66.16/67.28 and PM10 has mean/median 83.20/85.78 µg/m³.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
text:
Across paired rows, Pearson correlation is 0.883 and Spearman correlation is
0.873. Mean absolute difference is 17.06, median absolute difference 16.80,
and RMSE 23.05 µg/m³. The median PM10:PM2.5 ratio is 1.435 (mean 1.272).
Absolute differences are within 1, 2, and 5 µg/m³ for 30.6%, 36.8%, and
40.1% of pairs; relative differences are within 5%, 10%, and 20% for 39.4%,
40.0%, and 40.1%. Only one pair is exactly equal (0.072%); one pair has
PM10 below PM2.5 (0.072%). Absolute-difference percentiles (50th/90th/95th/
99th/maximum) are 16.80/37.56/41.38/47.87/60.36 µg/m³.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
text:
The largest absolute gap is 2023-06-06 (PM2.5 136.59, PM10 196.95; gap
60.36 µg/m³). The smallest is 2025-03-01 (both 93.554; the single exact
equality). These results support `accurate/plausible` for independent mappings:
the lines co-move, as particulate measures can, but are not duplicates. The
co-movement is an interpretation of this model series, not a health or legal
conclusion; the approximately 45 km grid and daily averaging limit local
inference.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
text:
The visual near-overlap is concentrated in the 92-row recent refresh: its
Pearson correlation is 0.997, median gap 1.89 µg/m³, and median ratio 1.022.
The 1,295 Zenodo rows have correlation 0.895, median gap 19.66 µg/m³, and
median ratio 1.436. The repository code does not alias the variables, but the
sharp change between source segments is not explained by the Zenodo metadata;
model version, domain selection, or upstream processing may have changed.
Treat the merged file as two provenance segments rather than a fully
homogeneous instrument series until that upstream continuity is documented.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
publisher: Open-Meteo / CAMS Global; deposited dataset by Nitiraj Kulkarni and Jagadish Tawade
section_path: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality > Audit of the retained file (1,387 paired daily rows)
text:
The quality diagnostic flags near-identity, a PM10-below-PM2.5 rate above 5%,
or the combination of correlation at least 0.99999 and mean absolute
difference below 0.01 µg/m³. None is present in the retained file.
title: Jakarta historical PM2.5 and PM10 series: provenance and quality

heading_path: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality
publisher: Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta / Dinas Lingkungan Hidup
section_path: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality
text:
Jakarta's air-pollution strategy combines governance and monitoring, reduction
of emissions from mobile sources, and reduction from stationary sources. The
intervention set includes public transport and vehicle-emission testing,
low-emission zones, cleaner energy and fuels, industrial and power-plant
monitoring, construction-dust control, open-burning and waste controls, green
infrastructure, and better public disclosure.
title: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality

heading_path: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality
publisher: Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta / Dinas Lingkungan Hidup
section_path: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality
text:
The city also promotes low-emission mobility such as public transport, walking,
and cycling when conditions are suitable. These actions complement—rather than
replace—regulation and enforcement of industrial, energy, transport, and waste
sources. A modelled reduction or policy target must not be presented as an
observed reduction unless a suitable evaluation measured it.
title: Ways to improve Jakarta air quality

text:
Pergub DKI No. 66/2020 is listed as berlaku by both BPK and DKI JDIH and
became effective 2020-12-24. It requires emission testing arrangements for
motor vehicles and sets inspection/control responsibilities. PP No. 22/2021
and Permen LHK No. 14/2020 are national instruments for ambient environmental

section_path: Why rules can coexist with poor air: implementation evidence > What implementation evidence actually says
text:
In its 2024 public statement, DKI said implementation of Kepgub 576/2023's
Strategy for Air Pollution Control was still being completed: the city was
developing a more systematic emissions inventory, tightening mobile and
stationary-source oversight, and seeking cooperation with Bogor, Depok,
Tangerang, Bekasi, and Cianjur. DKI's official CEMS page publishes stationary-
source monitoring/evaluation reports for 2020–2024. These are evidence of
program activity and identified needs, not proof that all sources comply or
that pollution fell because of one measure.

section_path: Why rules can coexist with poor air: implementation evidence > What implementation evidence actually says
text:
The DKI emissions-testing FAQ says testing is mandatory for passenger cars and
motorcycles older than three years under Pergub 66/2020 and that failure can
lead to a traffic ticket under national traffic law. [jakarta-emission-testing]
A DKI/Vital Strategies
2024 survey report discusses barriers and support for enforcement; it is
attitudinal evidence, not a compliance rate. The public pages reviewed here do
not provide a complete, independently audited denominator for all vehicles,
all industrial stacks, inspection frequency, or sanction follow-through. Those
are material evidence gaps. [jakarta-cems-monitoring]

text:
The official Supreme Court case directory records citizen lawsuit
374/Pdt.G/LH/2019/PN Jkt.Pst (decision 2021-09-16). [jakarta-court-air-quality]
It is evidence of a court
finding about public duties and regional coordination; it is not evidence that
every ordered action was completed. DKI itself describes regional transport,
industry, meteorology, and airshed contributions, so a Jakarta-only rule may
have limited effect when emissions originate outside the province. This is a
mechanism and governance constraint, not proof that any single agency caused
a particular reading.

heading_path: Evidence-based policy improvements for Jakarta
jurisdiction: Jakarta and the Greater Jakarta airshed
publisher: Dinas Lingkungan Hidup DKI Jakarta; World Health Organization
section_path: Evidence-based policy improvements for Jakarta
text:
* Near term enforcement: publish a vehicle-testing denominator and pass/fail
  and sanction rates; expand roadside checks and repair support; audit testing
  centres; require transparent stationary-source inspection and CEMS follow-up.
  DKI's own 2024 materials identify inventory and oversight as work in
  progress, so report completion rather than announce activity as impact.
* Transport: make public transport reliable and affordable, target the
  dirtiest high-use vehicles, control idling and freight routes, and evaluate
  low-emission zones or road pricing with an enacted legal basis, exemptions,
  equity protections, and measured emissions—not only traffic speed.
* Industry and power: enforce permits and stack standards, publish CEMS and
  inspection data, investigate coal and industrial contributions, and use
  corrective orders and sanctions with follow-through. Attribution must retain
  uncertainty across source-apportionment studies.
* Regional coordination: use one airshed inventory and synchronized plans with
  Bogor, Depok, Tangerang, Bekasi, and Cianjur; include meteorology and
  upwind industrial sources. A Jakarta-only intervention cannot control every
  transported plume.
* Monitoring and transparency: add calibrated stations and open timestamped
  raw data, QA/QC, station siting, missingness, emissions inventories, and
  programme evaluations. Keep ISPU, PM2.5 concentration, and health indicators
  distinct.
* Health protection: publish clear episode thresholds and advice, prioritize
  schools, outdoor workers, older adults, children, and people with heart/lung
  disease, and make clean indoor air available. WHO stresses that these
  personal measures are a supplement; source reduction remains the primary,
  equitable intervention.
title: Evidence-based policy improvements for Jakarta

heading_path: High-rise and ground-level exposure
publisher: Research literature; geographic scope must be checked per study
section_path: High-rise and ground-level exposure
text:
Some street-canyon studies observe lower particulate concentrations at greater
heights, but the relationship is not universal. Road distance, building and
street geometry, wind, nearby stacks, window opening, ventilation, filtration,
indoor sources, and time spent outdoors can dominate the result.
title: High-rise and ground-level exposure

heading_path: High-rise and ground-level exposure
publisher: Research literature; geographic scope must be checked per study
section_path: High-rise and ground-level exposure
text:
Evidence from another city or building cannot automatically be generalized to
Jakarta. A rooftop monitoring station is not the same as pedestrian-level
exposure, and a high apartment floor is not automatically safer. Answers must
state the study location, measurement height, indoor/outdoor setting, pollutant,
and limitations. Exact sensor height should only be reported when official
station metadata supplies it.
title: High-rise and ground-level exposure

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Purpose and legal status
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Purpose and legal status
text: WHO describes the 2021 Global Air Quality Guidelines as health-based recommendations and interim targets for key pollutants. Governments may use them as targets while considering technical capacity, economic capacity, air-quality policy and local political and social conditions.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Purpose and legal status
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Purpose and legal status
text: The guidelines are not Indonesian legislation and do not change the legal status of a national or DKI standard. An answer should label a comparison as a health-guideline comparison, not as a finding that a Jakarta operator violated Indonesian law.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Recommended particulate levels
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Recommended particulate levels
text: The WHO table reports a PM2.5 annual guideline level of 5 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour guideline level of 15 micrograms per cubic metre. The 24-hour recommendation is defined at the 99th percentile, equivalent to approximately three to four exceedance days per year.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Recommended particulate levels
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Recommended particulate levels
text: For PM10, the table reports an annual guideline level of 15 micrograms per cubic metre and a 24-hour guideline level of 45 micrograms per cubic metre. These values use an averaging time and pollutant-specific unit that must remain attached to the comparison.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Interim targets and uncertainty
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Interim targets and uncertainty
text: WHO provides interim targets as progressive steps for places where pollution is high. The guideline does not state that concentrations below a threshold have zero health effects; it is a population-health recommendation and should not be used to diagnose an individual.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Interim targets and uncertainty
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets > Interim targets and uncertainty
text: The guideline page says the 2021 update reflects stronger evidence of health effects at lower concentrations than earlier guidance. Source apportionment, exposure and intervention decisions still require local data and methods; the guideline alone does not identify Jakarta's emission sources.
title: WHO Global Air Quality Guidelines (2021) — particulate matter targets

heading_path: WHO air-quality guideline context
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO air-quality guideline context
text:
WHO air-quality guideline levels are health-based recommendations for pollutants
including PM2.5, PM10, ozone, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and carbon
monoxide. They are not Indonesian legal standards. Answers should state which
framework is being used when comparing a measurement with a threshold.
title: WHO air-quality guideline context

heading_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Purpose
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Purpose
text: The WHO Q&A addresses personal interventions and risk communication for air pollution. It presents exposure-reduction options as public-health advice and does not replace emission-control policy or clinical care.
title: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024)

heading_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Exposure reduction
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Exposure reduction
text: The guidance emphasizes checking air-quality information and reducing exposure during pollution episodes, including adjusting strenuous outdoor activity when conditions are poor. The appropriate action depends on the pollutant, duration, activity and vulnerability of the person.
title: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024)

heading_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Exposure reduction
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Exposure reduction
text: Indoor measures can reduce exposure when outdoor air is polluted, but indoor sources and ventilation conditions matter. A room or cleaner should not be described as automatically safe without considering filtration, airflow, maintenance, occupancy and indoor combustion.
title: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024)

heading_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Respirator boundary
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Respirator boundary
text: Particulate respirators can reduce inhaled particles when they are appropriate for the pollutant and fit well. They do not filter every gas, fit varies, and they are not a substitute for reducing emissions. Advice for people with heart or lung disease should be individualized by a clinician.
title: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024)

heading_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Risk communication
publisher: World Health Organization
section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Risk communication
text: The Q&A is a general communication source, not a diagnosis tool. An assistant should state the date and limits of the advice, distinguish population guidance from individual medical advice, and escalate severe symptoms to appropriate urgent care.
title: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024)

section_path: WHO personal interventions and risk communication (2024) > Locator note
